observation_summary: Calling mapper.setDateFormat() unexpectedly changes the ObjectMapper's configured TimeZone to the JVM default, whereas it previously preserved the existing TimeZone configuration.
hypothesis: The implementation of setDateFormat() incorrectly overwrites the existing TimeZone configuration in the BaseSettings object by extracting the TimeZone from the provided DateFormat object, even when the user has explicitly set a different TimeZone on the mapper.
prediction: The code in BaseSettings (or the method handling setDateFormat) will be found to perform an assignment like 'this.timeZone = dateFormat.getTimeZone()' without checking if the TimeZone was already explicitly configured or if it should be preserved.
experiment_rationale: The bug report explicitly states that the behavior changed between versions and that the fix involves 'trying to retain existing configured time zone and not taking it from DateFormat'. This confirms the root cause is an incorrect assignment/initialization logic.
reasoning_summary: The defect is a classic case of an incorrect value assignment. The system is overwriting a previously set, valid state (the TimeZone) with a value derived from a new input (the DateFormat) that should not have overridden the existing configuration. This is not a missing check (Checking) or a procedural logic error (Algorithm/Method), but rather an incorrect state update.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: The issue is not the procedure of setting the date format, but the side-effect of overwriting a state variable (TimeZone) that should have remained unchanged.
While a check could prevent the overwrite, the root cause is the incorrect assignment logic itself, not a missing validation of input parameters.
